query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor aluminum (Al) additions to a Ti–Ni primary HEA will induce the in‐situ formation of an ordered γ′ (Ni3(Ti,Al))-type precipitate phase within a disordered γ matrix, thereby significantly enhancing its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni based high-entropy alloy that initially forms a disordered single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Introduce 3–5 atomic percent Al into the Ti–Ni HEA, followed by a controlled heat treatment designed to promote the precipitation of the γ′ phase.
generation.conditions: Test at elevated temperatures (approximately 800–1000 °C) where ordering and precipitation occur.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent, nanoscale γ′ precipitates (of approximate Ni3(Ti,Al) stoichiometry) embedded in a disordered γ matrix, resulting in a dual-phase microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The addition of Al drives an ordering reaction that results in the in-situ formation of γ′ precipitates. These precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and enhance creep resistance, thereby improving yield strength and high-temperature performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable improvement in high-temperature yield strength (at least a 10% increase) and improved creep resistance relative to the baseline Ti–Ni HEA.
generation.baseline: Ti–Ni primary HEA with no Al addition, exhibiting a disordered single-phase structure.
generation.boundary: Al content strictly limited to 3–5 at%; beneficial effects are expected in the temperature window of 800–1000 °C with proper heat-treatment parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of γ′ precipitation and its long-term stability under service conditions must be determined experimentally; thermodynamic predictions based on similar Ni-based systems support the mechanism, but compositional differences may yield deviations.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one baseline Ti–Ni HEA and one with 4 at% Al. After a standardized heat treatment at 900 °C, perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests. Use XRD and high-resolution TEM to confirm the presence, morphology, and volume fraction of the γ′ phase.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification via XRD/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added alloy does not develop a coherent γ′ phase or fails to show at least a 10% improvement in yield strength or creep resistance relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In particular, the extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness of FCC-structured HEAs at ambient temperature and cryogenic temperatures have garnered significant attention [,,,,]. The low yield strength of FCC-structured HEAs, which is typically just 200 MPa in the as-cast form, is a significant disadvantage, as it is significantly less than the necessary strength of metallic structural materials [,]. To overcome these limitations in mechanical properties, a proposed method is to manufacture an HEA composed of a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix with an ordered FCC structure (L12) precipitated phase, i.e., the γ′ phase, by adding Al + Ti. An HEA based on a γ + γ′ alloy system exhibited excellent thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength retention around a temperature of 800 °C [,,,]. The γ′ phase is an ordered phase with an almost exact stoichiometric composition ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, with γ′ depending on the Al + Ti content []. Numerous studies have been conducted on the γ′ phase’s formation and mechanical properties [,]. A high content of Al + Ti leads to the formation of precipitate phases such as Ni2AlTi. Most research on HEAs has focused on evaluating their fundamental properties by creating ingots through arc melting and casting []. HEAs require a rapid cooling rate to achieve single-phase solid solutions [,]. As the size of the HEA increases, differences in the internal and external cooling rates make it challenging to maintain uniform microstructures, thus limiting the scalability of HEAs []. Additive manufacturing (AM), which completes processes in a relatively short time, is well suited for producing HEAs [,,,]. Direct energy deposition (DED) is commonly employed in AM []. The fast solidification rate of DED is beneficial for grain refinement and can prevent component segregation []. Additionally, the efficient heat source in DED results in a narrow heat-affected zone (HAZ) and a low dilution rate of the base material. These characteristics primarily reduce cracks, deformations, and metallurgical changes in the base metal, leading to fewer defects and improved production quality compared to other methods []. Therefore, through the application of the DED process in the AM of HEAs, HEAs with excellent performance can be produced with a very high production efficiency [,].
